Here is a puzzle in a small 2D grid language called Littleman, used by the ICFP Programming Contest 2026. It is NOT a language you know - the complete spec is below and is verified against the real judge, so trust it over your priors.

=== LANGUAGE SPEC ===
## The language

Grid of ASCII. Rooms are rectangles of `+` `-` `|`. A little man `@` spawns inside a room
**facing right**, executes the cell under him each tick, then steps one cell. Hitting a room
border is a fatal `wall` error. Registers: `A` main hand, `B` off hand, `BP` backpack — all
signed 64-bit, all starting 0. `BP` is **write-only**: you can branch on it, never read it.

| | |
|---|---|
| `0`–`9` | `A` = digit |
| `` `123` `` | literal; loads on the **closing** backtick. Walked backwards it reads backwards. Spaces inside are ignored |
| `M` / `W` | `B = A` / swap `A,B` |
| `+ - * / % N` | `A = A op B`; `/` floors and puts the **remainder in B**; `N` negates |
| `& \| ~ { }` | and, or, xor, `A<<B`, `A>>B` (arithmetic) |
| `> < ^ v` | set direction |
| `X` | turn by sign(A): right if >0, left if <0, straight if 0. `A` unchanged |
| `b m d a ] x` | `BP=A`; `BP-=1`; turn right/left if `BP>0`; `BP>>=1`; `x` turns right if low bit set else left |
| `q` | `BP` = number of values in the nearest incoming pipe |
| `s S` | send `A` to nearest / every outgoing pipe (blocks if full) |
| `r R U` | receive into `A` from nearest / any incoming pipe; `U` also turns away from that side |
| `Y` | split into two men moving perpendicular; both inherit `A,B,BP` |
| `H` `.` space | halt; nop; nop |

I/O rooms are 3×3 holding a single `I` or `O`, each with exactly one pipe.
Input arrives one value per tick into the input pipe's source cell.

## Pipes — read this twice, it cost us a whole submission

A pipe **must start with an arrowhead whose backward cell is on the source room's border**,
and **ends at the first arrowhead whose forward cell is on another room's border**.

- `>>` — shortest legal pipe (2 cells, arrowheads at both ends).
- `--->` — **NOT A PIPE.** It starts with a body glyph. The program loads clean and then every
  test dies `no-pipe`.
- Body glyphs must match direction (`-` horizontal, `|` vertical); every bend is an arrowhead
  pointing the new way; the terminal arrowhead doubles as the final bend.

`s`/`r`/`q` use the **nearest** pipe by Manhattan distance from the instruction to the pipe
segment touching your room, ties broken in reading order. `R`/`U` take from any ready pipe.

## Backticks pair down COLUMNS as well as along rows

Within a column they pair top-to-bottom, 1st-2nd, 3rd-4th. **A non-digit between a vertical
pair is a load error** — this killed a program that was otherwise perfect:

```
expected a digit or a space between backticks, but found 's' at (2, 2)
```

If you lay literals in a grid, either keep backtick columns identical on every row (pad tokens
so they are symmetric, e.g. `` ` `NNN`s `` ` has backticks at offsets 1 and 5 **both** walked
left-to-right and right-to-left), or keep only spaces/digits between vertical pairs.
`sim.py` enforces this rule, so trust it.

## Scoring — layout matters more than instruction count

`score = max(width, height)² × avgTicks`, **lower is better**, and every case must pass.
Problems marked `footprint` ignore ticks entirely.

The bounding box dominates. Our Triangle went **5819 → 1500** with the *same ten instructions*,
purely by folding a flat 23×3 line into a 7×10 snake with the I/O rooms side by side:

```
+-+ +-+
|I| |O|
+-+ +-+
 v   ^
 v   ^
+-----+
|@rM*v|
|v1W+<|
|>W}sH|
+-----+
```

Get it **correct first**, then square it up. A correct big program beats a beautiful broken one.

## Useful patterns

- **No third register.** With only `A` and `B` readable, a loop that needs a constant *and* an
  accumulator *and* a temp needs external storage — use a pipe to a helper room as memory,
  or restructure the arithmetic. Triangle avoids a division entirely by computing
  `(n²+n) >> 1`, parking the `1` in `B` with two `W` swaps.
- **Pipes are FIFO queues** and hold one value per cell — a long pipe is a delay line and a
  bounded buffer. A ring of two rooms joined by pipes both ways is a rotatable store.
- **`BP` is a loop counter**: `b` to set, `m` to decrement, `d`/`a` to branch while positive.
- **Encode a stack in one integer** when the alphabet is small: push = `A*k + item`,
  pop = `%k` then `/k`. 64 bits holds 31 items at k=4.

## The LM-75 display (needed only for display problems)

A display is a special room drawn with `+` corners, `:` vertical walls, `=` horizontal walls.
Max interior 64x64. It is driven entirely by which SIDE a pipe attaches to:

* **Top pipe = ADDR.** Write `row*width + column` to move the cursor. Out-of-range is an error.
* **Left pipe = DATA.** Write a colour 0..15 to paint the pixel at the cursor, then the cursor
  advances (next column, else next row, else back to top-left). Any other value is an error.
* **Bottom pipe = SWAP.** Write `0` to copy next->current, clear next and reset the cursor;
  write `1` to copy next->current but keep the cursor and next. Any other value is an error.

Attaching two pipes to one side, a pipe to the right side, or a pipe to a corner is a load error.
Within a tick the display processes ADDR, then DATA, then SWAP. Cursor starts at 0,0; both
buffers start colour 0 (black).


=== A WORKING EXAMPLE (accepted 19/19) ===
Triangle: read n, output n(n+1)/2 as (n*n + n) >> 1.

+-+ +-+
|I| |O|
+-+ +-+
 v   ^
 v   ^
+-----+
|@rM*v|
|v1W+<|
|>W}sH|
+-----+

Walk order r M * + W 1 W } s H. The man enters at @ heading right; running onto v turns him down, < turns him west, and so on. The two W swaps park the constant 1 in B for the shift, because loading a literal always lands in A.

=== EVIDENCE THIS IS TRACTABLE ===
Using exactly this spec, seven problems have already been accepted by the judge:
Triangle 19/19, History Lesson 1/1, Reverse a List 20/20, Sort 25/25, Brackets 26/26,
Packet Reassembly 20/20, Sudoku Auditor 20/20. So the language is expressive enough;
the difficulty is bookkeeping, not missing primitives.

=== YOUR TASK ===
Problem: LLLM (slug little-little-little-man)

Interpret an LLLM program and show its state on a display.

## The LLLM Language

Little little littleman (LLLM) is a simple subset of the
[little littleman (LLM)](/problems/little-little-man) language, which is a
simple subset of the language that you have learned during the course. *All
valid LLLM programs are valid LLM programs, which are valid littleman
programs*. This problem will not recap the basics of littleman programs;
consult the [textbook](/textbook), [language
reference](/language-reference), and [editor](/editor) if you're confused.

LLLM programs run in a single room and have a single `@` designating the little
man's starting position. The `@` moves with the man: the cell where he started
is ordinary empty space, and walking back over it does nothing.

The full set of operations in the LLLM language is:
- `^` `>` `v` `<` — set heading to N / E / S / W
- `0`–`9` — `A = n`
- `M` — `B = A`
- `+` — `A = A + B`
- `-` — `A = A - B`
- `X` — turn clockwise if `A > 0`, counterclockwise if `A < 0`, don't turn if `A = 0`
- `H` — halt: the man stays on the `H` forever

On each tick the little man executes the operation he is standing on (if applicable)
and *then* advances in his current direction. The little man halts if he hits a wall:
he stays put on the wall cell forever, and frames committed after that show him drawn
on the wall cell. (This differs from littleman, where hitting a wall is an error.)

**The programs you receive will be well-formed:** every program will have a single
room with a single `@` inside. Other characters will either be spaces or valid operations.

## Drawing

Draw the LLLM program with its top-left corner at the top-left corner of your
[display](/grading#displays). Your display will be 16x16; if your LLLM program is smaller than that
leave the pixels outside of the program black.

You should use color `9` (bright red) to represent the current position of the
little man.  When the little man is on top of an instruction or a wall, draw
*him*, not the thing he is on top of.

Other cells have fixed colors similar to what you see in the editor:
- room walls — 4 (blue)
- `<` `>` `^` `v` `X` `H` — 3 (yellow)
- `0`–`9` — 8 (gray)
- `M` — 12 (bright blue)
- `+` `-` — 10 (bright green)
- space — 0 (black)

## Input and output

The first [round](/grading#round-based) supplies two integers `W H`
and then `W*H` [ASCII](/grading#ascii) values that comprise
a valid LLLM program, in row-major order (top row first, left to right).
Commit a single frame showing the starting state.

Subsequent rounds supply one integer `k`. Step the program forward `k` ticks
or until it halts, whichever comes first.  Then commit a single frame showing
the state of the program.

Test cases end after the round where the LLLM program halts.

I/O spec: {"input": {"of": {"repeat": "int"}, "note": "the first round is the LLLM program: W H, then W\u00b7H ASCII codes (row-major); every later round is one step command k"}, "display": {"width": 16, "height": 16}, "constraints": ["`4 \u2264 W, H \u2264 16`", "`1 \u2264 k \u2264 64`", "at most 30 rounds and at most 200 ticks per test case", "no step commands arrive after the program halts"]}
Scoring: footprint-tick  (score = max(width,height)^2 * avgTicks, lower is better)
Constraints: `4 ≤ W, H ≤ 16`; `1 ≤ k ≤ 64`; at most 30 rounds and at most 200 ticks per test case; no step commands arrive after the program halts

  round 1 in = ["64"]

  round 4 in = ["64"]

=== WHAT I WANT BACK ===
Work out the algorithm in prose first, then give the finished grid as a single fenced code block with exact spacing (every line padded to the same width). Remember only A and B are readable (BP is write-only and branch-only), so extra state must live in pipes used as FIFOs or as a rotatable two-room ring.

Be rigorous about these, the usual causes of failure:
  * a pipe must START with an arrowhead whose backward cell touches the source room border and END at an arrowhead whose forward cell touches another room border; '--->' is not a pipe.
  * backticks pair down COLUMNS as well as along rows; a non-digit between a vertical pair is a load error.
  * walking into a room border kills the man instantly.

If you cannot finish a correct grid, say exactly where you got stuck instead of presenting an untested one.


=== NOTES FROM PREVIOUS ATTEMPTS (read these) ===
An earlier attempt at this problem produced a 903 x 586 grid that the official judge accepted as
LOADABLE and scored 6 of 21 test cases. So a grid of that shape is fine and the layout approach
works — what was missing was correct behaviour, largely because that attempt was never shown the
expected display `frames` (my earlier prompt wrongly showed `out=[]` and truncated the inputs).
The complete frames are given above. Use them.

Two facts that cost previous attempts a lot of time:
  * An LM-75 DISPLAY room is drawn with '+' corners, '=' horizontal borders and ':' vertical
    borders — the display analogue of '-' and '|'. Pipes are SUPPOSED to end on those glyphs.
    Verified against two judge-accepted programs (plotter 20/20, snake 17/17).
  * Size: up to roughly 1,000 x 1,000 is fine. Only an enormous grid is refused — 2,213 x 12,834
    was rejected with `413 payload_too_large`.

Optimise for FINISHING over elegance. Two prior runs spent their whole budget on a beautiful
design and produced no grid at all, which is worth nothing. Generate the grid programmatically
with python, get it loading first, then make cases pass one at a time.

DELIVERY: write the program with python to /mnt/data/lllm_v7.man — verbatim grid, one line per
row, no fences, single trailing newline. Report which public cases pass. If it is incomplete,
still write the best LOADABLE grid you have and say which behaviours are wrong.



=== WHERE THIS PROBLEM ACTUALLY STANDS, AND THE ONE THING THAT WILL MOVE IT ===
Three attempts have been submitted to the official judge. The best result, twice over, is:

    Passed 10/21
    Passed all 10 public tests
    Failed 11 of 11 private tests (10 wrong-frames, 1 step-cap)

Read that carefully: the interpreter is correct on **every case it can see** and wrong on
**every case it cannot**. Making the public cases pass is no longer useful — they already do.
The entire remaining problem is generalisation to inputs you have never been shown.

So please do NOT hand-check the public cases again. Instead do differential testing:

  1. Write a reference implementation of the interpreted language's semantics in ordinary Python
     — a straightforward, obviously-correct simulator, no cleverness.
  2. Write a random program generator that samples the WHOLE declared constraint space, not the
     shapes the public cases happen to use:
         ["`4 \u2264 W, H \u2264 16`", "`1 \u2264 k \u2264 64`", "at most 30 rounds and at most 200 ticks per test case", "no step commands arrive after the program halts"]
     Deliberately generate the awkward corners: minimum and maximum sizes, non-square grids, the
     maximum number of rooms and pipes, men that block on a full pipe, men that halt while others
     keep running, a man hitting a wall, negative values, values at the extremes of the allowed
     range, and the maximum round count.
  3. Also write a simulator for the OUTER littleman language so you can execute your generated
     .man grid directly.
  4. Run both on a few hundred random programs and compare the display frames tick by tick. Every
     mismatch is one of the 10 wrong-frames failures, reproduced locally where you can debug it.
  5. Fix, regenerate, repeat until random testing is clean.

The `1 step-cap` failure is separate and smaller: one case exceeds the step budget, so make the
per-tick common path cheaper for the largest inputs.

Constraints you can rely on, measured against the real judge: area is nearly free (a 9.4 MB grid
was accepted; only 11 MB+ was refused), and ticks are cheap (accepted programs average 1.5
million per case). The previous grid was only 390 x 420, so you have enormous headroom for both.

DELIVERY: /mnt/data/lllm_v7.man — verbatim grid, one line per row, no fences, single trailing
newline. Write it as soon as it loads and rewrite it as you improve, so a truncated reply still
leaves a submittable file. Report what your random testing found.
